universal set is ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following shaded regions represents the truth set of the predicate?" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})$ is the set of $n$-tuples in its universal set $U={U}_{1}\times {U}_{2}\times ⋯\times {U}_{n}$ such that substituting these tuples for the variables makes the predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\in U\,|\,P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $U={R}^{2}.$ We need to find $(x,y)\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ $4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}-36>0$ Let's first rearrange our inequality as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}-36 & >0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2} & >36 \\ \frac{4{x}^{2}}{36}+\frac{9{y}^{2}}{36} & >1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & >1\end{aligned} $$ From here, we see that this represents an ellipse centered at $O$ with semi-axes $3$ and $2.$ Finally, let's sketch the truth set $T$ of :question/id #uuid "34f7a331-3a09-5214-b793-a1233bb14dc6" :question/math-academy-id "q-162827" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=-2$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.16$ | $0.09$ | $0.05$ | | $X=1$ | $0.44$ | $0.21$ | $0.05$ | The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given above, while the marginal mass functions for these variables are shown below.
$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.3$ $0.7$

$y$ $-2$ $0$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.3$ $0.1$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=0)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if $$ f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) $$ for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.09.$ On the other hand, $$ P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09.\,✓ $$ - Statement II is false. Checking some possible products, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}f(0,-2) & =0.16\ne 0.3\cdot 0.6={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(-2) & \times \end{aligned} $$ So, $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$ - Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-287256f7-b082-5a2a-854b-414b7b8a37a2"] :db/ensure 17592186161704 :question/problem "Workers of a small company decided to elect a new union representative. There are $50$ workers, and $60\%$ of this worker population will vote for candidate $A.$ Let the random variable $X_i$ be equal to ![](images/c2/c28a8c33f7c9beeb8132564b044489ff480065b047327bda1e8eae8a84218ca2.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ Find $P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0).$" :question/worked-solution "We have a population of size $N = 50,$ and $p = 0.6$ represents the proportion of the population that will vote for candidate $A.$ Therefore: - The number of members that will vote for candidate $A$ equals $$ Np = 50(0.6) = 30. $$ - The number of members that will *not* vote for candidate $A$ equals $$ N(1 - p) = 50(1 - 0.6) = 20. $$ We select two members of the population at random. We need to find $P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0),$ the probability that the second member will *not* vote for candidate $A$ given that the first member will *not* vote for candidate $A$ either. If the first member does *not* vote for candidate $A,$ we have $\qquad$ $N - 1 = 50 - 1 = 49$ members remaining, and $\qquad$ $N(1 - p)-1 = 19$ members remaining that will not vote for candidate $A.$ Therefore, $$ P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0) = \dfrac{N(1 - p)-1}{N-1} = \dfrac{19}{49}. $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion $p$ of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate $A.$" If the company has $N = 50$ employees, and $30$ of them will vote for candidate $A,$ then the proportion $p$ is given by $$ p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6. $$ In other words, $60\%$ of the company's employees will vote for candidate $A.$ Note the following: - $N$ is the **population size** - $p$ is the **population proportion** - The number of employees that will vote for candidate $A$ is given by $$ Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30. $$ In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating $p$ in cases where the population size $N$ is very large. Note that although the population size $N$ is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas. We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable $X_i,$ defined by ![](images/76/76b2ae3dd8206bfdbe208d0e037bd1efa5614101917cf6f981df078cb3cdc8cf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate $A$ is straightforward: $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{i}=1) & =\frac{\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A}{\text{population size}} \\ & =\frac{Np}{N} \\ & =\frac{30}{50} \\ & =0.6\end{aligned} $$ **Watch out!** It's important to note that the $X_i$'s are *dependent!* For example, $$ P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ). $$ To see why, note that $P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,$ as before. However, $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{(\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A)-1}{\text{population size}-1} \\ & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\ & =\frac{50\cdot 0.6-1}{50-1} \\ & =\frac{30-1}{49} \\ & =\frac{29}{49} \\ & ≈0.592 \\ & \ne P({X}_{2}=1).\end{aligned} $$ Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate $A.$ So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will *also* vote for candidate $A,$ we consider a reduced population with $N-1 = 49$ members, of which only $30-1 = 29$ will vote for candidate $A.$ Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$ Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*. This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. To see why, we first note that $$ P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5. $$ Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\ & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\ & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\ & =\frac{499}{999} \\ & ≈0.5.\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we've shown that $$ P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1), $$ suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size. The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. Let's now consider the following statistic: $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i $$ where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following: - Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ - Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables. - It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore, $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p). $$ We summarize this process using the following flow chart. ![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png) Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations: $$ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p) $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore, $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p). $$ Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows: $$ \widehat{\,p} = \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i = \overline{X} $$ Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that $$ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p). $$ Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\ & =p.\end{aligned} $$ For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\ & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we have the following important results: $$ \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} $$ It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$ is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$ $$ \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}} $$ If $p$ is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate $\widehat{\,p}$ in the standard error formula, as follows: $$ \widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}} $$ Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162231 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id black]{\phantom{XX}}\,\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$" :question/worked-solution "Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $\mathbf x(t_0)$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ![](images/7b/7b64128fdaf3565ee121779a8fcd2c84db8f639ded96f0884d6ad7e728c83b1c.svg) So, $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}3(t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that ![](images/7f/7f1779e39ecb5e2bcce580d20a85eae97be505e2ad0987fa45b5b9e22c52fbbf.svg) So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3(t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230191 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving *inhomogeneous systems* of ODEs as well. Consider the system $$ \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t), $$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, and suppose we are given an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$. Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system. First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t) $$ and differentiate it using the product rule: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\ & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\ & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\ & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned} $$ Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get $$ \mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the solution to our IVP is $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*. Let's see some concrete examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229257 :activity/expected-seconds 1440.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id \mathbf{a}_n \}$** as $$ \Vert{ \color{purple} \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} }\Vert. $$ We can also define the **angle between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$** to be the acute angle $\theta$ between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ as shown in the diagram below. ![](images/07/07fa0d011bbfd49f89ddc5035a27839640a0c2624046d39fbfe8f57c476b5b25.png) Finally, notice that we can represent the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of two orthogonal vectors: $$ \mathbf{x} = \underbrace{\textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x}}_{\large \in S} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x})}_{\large \in S^\perp} $$ **Note:** The vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :db/ensure where $\mathbf{x}_S=\text{proj}_S\,\mathbf{x}$ is in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\},$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ is in the orthogonal complement of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$. That is, $\mathbf{x}_S=k_1\mathbf{a}_1+k_2\mathbf{a}_2\in S\,$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp.$ From the equation above, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\ & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\ & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, using the fact that $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ is orthogonal to $S,$ and the fact that ={k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2} \\ & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2} \\ & Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=0)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if $$ f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) $$ for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.09.$ On the other hand, $$ P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09.\,✓ $$ - Statement II is false. Checking some possible products, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}f(0,-2) & =0.16\ne 0.3\cdot 0.6={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(-2) & \times \end{aligned} $$ So, $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$ - Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent. 17592186161704 :question/problem "Workers of a small company decided to elect a new union representative. There are $50$ workers, and $60\%$ of this worker population will vote for candidate $A.$ Let the random variable $X_i$ be equal to ![](images/c2/c28a8c33f7c9beeb8132564b044489ff480065b047327bda1e8eae8a84218ca2.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ Find $P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0).$" :question/worked-solution "We have a population of size $N = 50,$ and $p = 0.6$ represents the proportion of the population that will vote for candidate $A.$ Therefore: - The number of members that will vote for candidate $A$ equals $$ Np = 50(0.6) = 30. $$ - The number of members that will *not* vote for candidate $A$ equals $$ N(1 - p) = 50(1 - 0.6) = 20. $$ We select two members of the population at random. We need to find $P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0),$ the probability that the second member will *not* vote for candidate $A$ given that the first member will *not* vote for candidate $A$ either. If the first member does *not* vote for candidate $A,$ we have $\qquad$ $N - 1 = 50 - 1 = 49$ members remaining, and $\qquad$ $N(1 - p)-1 = 19$ members remaining that will not vote for candidate $A.$ Therefore, $$ P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0) = \dfrac{N(1 - p)-1}{N-1} = \dfrac{19}{49}. $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion $p$ of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate $A.$" If the company has $N = 50$ employees, and $30$ of them will vote for candidate $A,$ then the proportion $p$ is given by $$ p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6. $$ In other words, $60\%$ of the company's employees will vote for candidate $A.$ Note the following: - $N$ is the **population size** - $p$ is the **population proportion** - The number of employees that will vote for candidate $A$ is given by $$ Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30. $$ In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating $p$ in cases where the population size $N$ is very large. Note that although the population size $N$ is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas. We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable $X_i,$ defined by ![](images/76/76b2ae3dd8206bfdbe208d0e037bd1efa5614101917cf6f981df078cb3cdc8cf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate $A$ is straightforward: $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{i}=1) & =\frac{\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A}{\text{population size}} \\ & =\frac{Np}{N} \\ & =\frac{30}{50} \\ & =0.6\end{aligned} $$ **Watch out!** It's important to note that the $X_i$'s are *dependent!* For example, $$ P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ). $$ To see why, note that $P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,$ as before. However, $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{(\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A)-1}{\text{population size}-1} \\ & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\ & =\frac{50\cdot 0.6-1}{50-1} \\ & =\frac{30-1}{49} \\ & =\frac{29}{49} \\ & ≈0.592 \\ & \ne P({X}_{2}=1).\end{aligned} $$ Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate $A.$ So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will *also* vote for candidate $A,$ we consider a reduced population with $N-1 = 49$ members, of which only $30-1 = 29$ will vote for candidate $A.$ Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$ Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*. This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. To see why, we first note that $$ P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5. $$ Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\ & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\ & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\ & =\frac{499}{999} \\ & ≈0.5.\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we've shown that $$ P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1), $$ suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size. The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. Let's now consider the following statistic: $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i $$ where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following: - Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ - Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables. - It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore, $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p). $$ We summarize this process using the following flow chart. ![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png) Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations: $$ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p) $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore, $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p). $$ Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows: $$ \widehat{\,p} = \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i = \overline{X} $$ Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that $$ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p). $$ Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\ & =p.\end{aligned} $$ For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\ & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we have the following important results: $$ \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} $$ It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163349 :tutorial/content "The standard deviation of $\widehat{\,p}$ is called the **standard error** of $\widehat{\,p}$ and is denoted $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}$ $$ \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}} $$ If $p$ is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate $\widehat{\,p}$ in the standard error formula, as follows: $$ \widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}} $$ Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an estimate of $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162231 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/3d/3db7e4a714d16b8f150bbca5fc9e60fdbf30da038e7dbf331dc317d6ec7c8c3c.svg) Fill in the blanks in the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ![](images/e7/e7b8344a953c494431f7c9594dbe6124e2e4264c3d58bc94fa383323fc85389d.svg) where ![](images/d3/d3a5e4fd69f446e59007f8e3f8c982b424deedcb837670b75c5342968b7e0549.svg)* $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\,\,\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{XXXX}}\, \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ \,\,\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{XX}}\,\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$" :question/worked-solution "Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where $\mathbf x(t_0)$ is the initial condition vector. Let's evaluate each part separately: - First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ![](images/7b/7b64128fdaf3565ee121779a8fcd2c84db8f639ded96f0884d6ad7e728c83b1c.svg) So, $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}3(t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ - Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that ![](images/7f/7f1779e39ecb5e2bcce580d20a85eae97be505e2ad0987fa45b5b9e22c52fbbf.svg) So, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3(t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230191 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving *inhomogeneous systems* of ODEs as well. Consider the system $$ \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t), $$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, and suppose we are given an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$. Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system. First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t) $$ and differentiate it using the product rule: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\ & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\ & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\ & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned} $$ Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get $$ \mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the solution to our IVP is $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*. [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135088 :tutorial/content "Let $n,m$ be positive integers such that $n\leq m.$ Given an orthogonal set $\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\} \subset \Bbb R^m$ and a vector $\mathbf x \in \Bbb R^m,$ we define the **distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the vector space $S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$** as $$ \Vert{ \color{purple} \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} }\Vert. $$ We can also define the **angle between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$** to be the acute angle $\theta$ between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ as shown in the diagram below. ![](images/07/07fa0d011bbfd49f89ddc5035a27839640a0c2624046d39fbfe8f57c476b5b25.png) Finally, notice that we can represent the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of two orthogonal vectors: $$ \mathbf{x} = \underbrace{\textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x}}_{\large \in S} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x})}_{\large \in S^\perp} $$ **Note:** The vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135087 :tutorial/content "Let's now prove the formula for the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspaces $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1 \}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ given that $\mathbf{a}_1\perp \mathbf{a}_2.$ We start by writing $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of two vectors $$ \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}, $$ where $\mathbf{x}_S=\text{proj}_S\,\mathbf{x}$ is in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\},$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ is in the orthogonal complement of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$. That is, $\mathbf{x}_S=k_1\mathbf{a}_1+k_2\mathbf{a}_2\in S\,$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp.$ From the equation above, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\ & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\ & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, using the fact that $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ is orthogonal to $S,$ and the fact that $\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\mathbf{a}_2=0,$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0\end{aligned} & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}(x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2})\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ (x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2})\cdot {a}_{2}=0\end{aligned} \\ & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}x\cdot {a}_{1}-{k}_{1}({a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1})-{k}_{2}({a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{1})=0 \\ x\cdot {a}_{2}-{k}_{1}({a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{2})-{k}_{2}({a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2})=0\end{aligned} \\ & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}{k}_{1}({a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1})=x\cdot {a}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}({a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2})=x\cdot {a}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}{k}_{1}=\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}} \\ {k}_{2}=\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned} $$ As a result, we obtain our formula $$ \begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2} \\ & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2} \\ & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.\end{aligned} $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134002 :activity/expected-seconds 1320.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} \begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}-36 & >0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2} & >36 \\ \frac{4{x}^{2}}{36}+\frac{9{y}^{2}}{36} & >1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & >1\end{aligned} $$ From here, we see that :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=-2$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.16$ | $0.09$ | $0.05$ | | $X=1$ | $0.44$ | $0.21$ | $0.05$ | The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given above, while the marginal mass functions for these variables are shown below.
$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.3$ $0.7$

$y$ $-2$ $0$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.3$ $0.1$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=0)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent"] ["question-34f7a331-3a09-5214-b793-a1233bb14dc6" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if $$ f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) $$ for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.09.$ On the other hand, $$ P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09.\,✓ $$ - Statement II is false. Checking some possible products, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}f(0,-2) & =0.16\ne 0.3\cdot 0.6={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(-2) & \times \end{aligned} $$ So, $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$ - Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-34f7a331-3a09-5214-b793-a1233bb14dc6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-287256f7-b082-5a2a-854b-414b7b8a37a2" We need to find $P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0),$ the probability that the second member will *not* vote for candidate $A$ given that the first member will *not* vote for candidate $A$ either. If the first member does *not* vote for candidate $A,$ we have $\qquad$ $N - 1 = 50 - 1 = 49$ members remaining, and $\qquad$ $N(1 - p)-1 = 19$ members remaining that will not vote for candidate $A.$ Therefore, $$ P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0) = \dfrac{N(1 - p)-1}{N-1} = \dfrac{19}{49}. $$"] [17592186163344 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion $p$ of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate $A.$" If the company has $N = 50$ employees, and $30$ of them will vote for candidate $A,$ then the proportion $p$ is given by $$ p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6. $$ In other words, $60\%$ of the company's employees will vote for candidate $A.$ Note the following: - $N$ is the **population size** - $p$ is the **population proportion** - The number of employees that will vote for candidate $A$ is given by $$ Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30. $$ In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating $p$ in cases where the population size $N$ is very large. Note that although the population size $N$ is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas. We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable $X_i,$ defined by ![](images/76/76b2ae3dd8206bfdbe208d0e037bd1efa5614101917cf6f981df078cb3cdc8cf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,50.$ Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate $A$ is straightforward: $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{i}=1) & =\frac{\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A}{\text{population size}} \\ & =\frac{Np}{N} \\ & =\frac{30}{50} \\ & =0.6\end{aligned} $$ **Watch out!** It's important to note that the $X_i$'s are *dependent!* For example, $$ P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ). $$ To see why, note that $P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,$ as before. However, $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{(\text{the number of members that will vote for candidate }A)-1}{\text{population size}-1} \\ & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\ & =\frac{50\cdot 0.6-1}{50-1} \\ & =\frac{30-1}{49} \\ & =\frac{29}{49} \\ & ≈0.592 \\ & \ne P({X}_{2}=1).\end{aligned} $$ Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate $A.$ So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will *also* vote for candidate $A,$ we consider a reduced population with $N-1 = 49$ members, of which only $30-1 = 29$ will vote for candidate $A.$ Calculating $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)$ works similarly, as we'll see in the following example."] [17592186163346 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population of size $N=1\,000$ of which the proportion $p=0.5$ has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/a8/a801fdb0d37e38011713448593b185b440445d6a57b0ff42e00c21e66401f6bf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.$ Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the $X_i$'s are *dependent*. This time, however, since the population size $N = 1\,000$ is large, we may *approximate* that the $X_i$'s are *independent*. To see why, we first note that $$ P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5. $$ Now, computing $P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}P({X}_{2}=1|{X}_{1}=1) & =\frac{Np-1}{N-1} \\ & =\frac{1\,000\cdot 0.5-1}{1\,000-1} \\ & =\frac{500-1}{999} \\ & =\frac{499}{999} \\ & ≈0.5.\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we've shown that $$ P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1), $$ suggesting that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are (approximately) independent."] [17592186163345 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/32/32bc52b6268f6c5eeb9a6f07fff58c308871cc650541c16a4c595faf81e833df.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ It can be shown that the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables *provided that* the population size $N$ is *significantly larger* than the sample size $n$ (which we denote as $N \gg n$). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than $5\%$ of the population size. The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters. Let's now consider the following statistic: $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i $$ where $X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ Since the $X_i$'s take the value $1$ if the $i$th element has the characteristic or $0$ if the $i$th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic $X$ can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. We wish to determine the sampling distribution of $X.$ Note the following: - Each $X_i$ can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., $X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).$ - Since we're assuming that $N\gg n,$ it follows that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are (approximately) *independent and identically distributed* (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables. - It can be shown that a sum of $n$ I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p$ is a binomial random variable $B(n,p)$ (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore, $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p). $$ We summarize this process using the following flow chart. ![](images/f5/f50d54432c86d4b41ed842218a70b93617457de3e518aa88cbe6ea28762f37ea.png) Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations: $$ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p) $$"] [17592186163347 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows: ![](images/46/4624ca7ee7660803ddc7165252c3725030b13ab255f56dc5d87e23090c2363bf.svg) for $i = 1,\ldots,n.$ We know that if the population sample size $n$ is small compared to the population size $N,$ then the $X_i$'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore, $$ X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p). $$ Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an *estimate* for the population proportion $p$ as follows: $$ \widehat{\,p} = \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i = \overline{X} $$ Let's calculate the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p}.$ First, recall that $$ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p). $$ Therefore, for the mean of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{E}[\frac{X}{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot \text{E}[X] \\ & =\frac{1}{n}\cdot np \\ & =p.\end{aligned} $$ For the variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{X}{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot np(1-p) \\ & =\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we have the following important results: $$ \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} $$ It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is, it has mean $p$ and variance $\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.$"] [17592186163349 \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}} $$ If $p$ is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate $\widehat{\,p}$ in the standard error formula, as follows: $$ \widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}} $$ Note that we have written $\widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]$ to denote that the above expression is an Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system. First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t) $$ and differentiate it using the product rule: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\ & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\ & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\ & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned} $$ Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get $$ \mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have $$ \mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s. $$ Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the solution to our IVP is $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}}, $$ where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*. :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of a Predicate"}] :question/problem "Find the truth set of the following predicate:

$\qquad$ $P(x):$ $x^2+2x=3$

where the universal set is $\mathbb{Z}.$" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P(x)$ is the set of elements in its universal set $U$ such that substituting these elements for the variable makes the predicate a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ x \in U \: | \: P(x) \big\}
$$

The universal set for our predicate is $U = \mathbb{Z}.$

We need to find $x \in U$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $x^2+2x=3$

Now, we solve the above equation by factoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-3 & =0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-3\in\mathbb Z$ and $x=1\in\mathbb Z.$

Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is $T = \{-3,1\}.$"} {:db/id 17592186049002} {:db/id 17592186050035} {:db/id 17592186050073} {:db/id 17592186198700 :question/id #uuid $$
T=\{x\in U\,|\,P(x)\}
$$

The universal set for our predicate is $U=R.$

We need to find $x\in U$ such that the following is true:

$\,$ ${x}^{2}<9$

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & <9 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & <\sqrt{9} \\ |x| & <3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have

$$
-3\text{ }<x<3.
$$

where the universal set is $R.$" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P(x)$ is the set of elements in its universal set $U$ such that substituting these elements for the variable makes the predicate a true statement:

$$
T=\{x\in U\,|\,P(x)\}
$$

We need to find $x\in U$ such that the following is true:

$\,$ $5x+2>22$

The universal set for our predicate is $U=R.$

Now, we need to solve the above inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2>22 \\ 5x>20 \\ x>4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T=(4,\infty ).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198280 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198097 :question/id #uuid "14dc17f1-056e-5e82-81e6-c3964b7df2d2" :question/math-academy-id "e-12722"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aa2f2ccb-45b0-5d6a-aa94-ac3eb95c745b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198701 :question/id #uuid "5aac057d-91ad-5aae-a8c2-a1bdb997210f" :question/math-academy-id "q-171535"} {:db/id 17592186198721 :question/id #uuid "d3a9664a-054f-5dcf-9b0e-e1b4ab3dd171" :question/math-academy-id "q-174456"} {:db/id 17592186425980 :question/id #uuid "86866e7c-73c9-5409-8743-b71ad4d3cbe4" :question/math-academy-id "q-175366"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Predicates of More Than One Variable"} {:db/id 17592186198097 :question/id #uuid "14dc17f1-056e-5e82-81e6-c3964b7df2d2" :question/math-academy-id "e-12722" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198280 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aa2f2ccb-45b0-5d6a-aa94-ac3eb95c745b" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Predicates of More Than One Variable"}] :question/problem "Which of the following are mathematical predicates?

I. $x \geq y$

II. $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is a rational number.

III. $a$ is a positive number." :question/worked-solution "A *predicate* of the variables $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is a sentence that contains the variables defined on some *universal set,* and has the property that when we substitute concrete values for all the variables into the predicate, the result becomes a statement that is either true or false.

With that in mind, let's examine our options. 

- Option I is a predicate of two variables. Substituting a concrete pair of values $(x,y)$ into the sentence, we get a statement that is either true or false.

- Option II is a predicate of two variables. Substituting a concrete pair of values $(p,q)$ into the sentence, we get a statement that is either true or false.

- Option III is a predicate of one variable. Substituting a concrete value for $a$ into the sentence, we get a statement that is either true or false.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186198701 :question/id #uuid "5aac057d-91ad-5aae-a8c2-a1bdb997210f" :question/math-academy-id "q-171535"} {:db/id 17592186198721 - Option II is *not* a predicate. Substituting a concrete pair of values $(a,b)$ into the sentence, we do not get a statement that is either true or false.

$\qquad$ $p \, | \, q$, 

where the universal set is $\big\{ (p,q) \: | \: p = 1,2,6, \: q = 3,6,9 \big\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is the set of $n$-tuples in its universal set $U = U_1 \times U_2 \times \cdots \times U_n$ such that substituting these tuples for the variables makes the predicate a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \in U \: | \: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \big\}
$$

The universal set for our predicate is

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =\{1,2,6\}\times \{3,6,9\} \\  & =\{(1,3),(1,6),(1,9),(2,3),(2,6),(2,9),(6,3),(6,6),(6,9)\}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to find $(p,q) \in U$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $p \, | \, q$

The following pairs give the elements of our truth set:

- $(1,3)$ since $1$ divides $3,$

- $(1,6)$ since $1$ divides $6,$

- $(1,9)$ since $1$ divides $9,$

- $(2,6)$ since $2$ divides $6,$

- $(6,6)$ since $6$ divides $6.$

Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is

$$
T = \big\{ (1,3), (1,6), (1,9), (2,6), (6,6) \big\}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051063} {:db/id 17592186198702 :question/id #uuid "3f8ceacb-3e97-5937-aa19-3f06acd2a5eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-171536"} {:db/id 17592186198703 :question/id #uuid variable is a sentence that contains a variable defined on some universal set and has the property that when we substitute a concrete value of the variable into the predicate, the result becomes a mathematical statement that is either true or false.

The **truth set** $T$ of a predicate $P(x)$ is the set of elements in its universal set $U$ such that substituting these elements into the predicate gives a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ x \in U \: | \: P(x) \big\}
$$

For example, let's find the truth set of the following predicate:

$\qquad$ $D(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $2,$

where the universal set is $U = \big\{ 1,2, \ldots, 6 \big\}.$

To find the truth set $T,$ we need to find $x \in U$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $x$ is divisible by $2.$

Let's check all the elements in our universal set $U$ to determine which of them are elements of the truth set $T{:}$

- $x=1\notin T$ since $1$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=2\in T$ since $2$ is divisible by $2$

- $x=3\notin T$ since $3$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=4\in T$ since $4$ is divisible by $2$

- $x=5\notin T$ since $5$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=6\in T$ since $6$ is divisible by $2$

Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is

$$
T = \big\{ 2,4,6 \big\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8422ca20-ab2c-5e41-a789-3c21465dfc51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8139 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "dbb18ea5-8c55-58c8-81e5-4c923006baa2" :step/math-academy-id 153521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199092}} {:db/id 17592186199092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198279 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198096 :question/id #uuid "4b253527-f5ca-5927-97f0-d91491d598b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-12721"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c23caadd-1738-549f-aade-2c983dc250dc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049002} {:db/id 17592186050035} {:db/id 17592186050073}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198700} {:db/id 17592186198720} {:db/id 17592186425977} {:db/id 17592186425978}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of a Predicate"} :step/id #uuid "3cbfca6e-271d-50e8-8a2d-2854b810036b" :step/math-academy-id 153522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199093}} {:db/id 17592186199093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199540 :tutorial/content "A predicate of the variables $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is a sentence that contains these variables with the property that when we substitute concrete values for all the variables, the result becomes a statement that is either true or false. 

We can denote such a predicate using the following notation:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
$$

If $U_1$ is the universal set for $x_1,U_2$ is the universal set for $x_2,\ldots,$ etc, then the universal set $U$ for our predicate is given by the Cartesian product

$$
U = U_1 \times U_2 \times \cdots \times U_n.
$$

For example, the sentence

$\qquad$ $P(x,y): x+y \lt 2,$ $\quad$ $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$

is a predicate of two variables, $x$ and $y.$ In this case, the universal set is

$$
U = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

The **truth set** $T$ of a predicate $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is the set of $n$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) \in U$ such that substituting these tuples into the predicate gives a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \in U \: | \: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \big\}
$$

For example, to determine the truth set of the predicate $P(x,y)$ defined above, we need to find $(x,y) \in \mathbb R^2$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $x+y \lt 2$

To find the truth set, we first find an explicit condition on $y$ as a function of $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & <2 \\ y & <2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the truth set contains all tuples $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$ that satisfy this inequality. We can write the truth set $T$ of our predicate as follows:

$$
T = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \:|\: y < 2-x\big\}
$$

Finally, since $T$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^2,$ we can represent it as a region in the coordinate plane.

\begin{aligned}x+y & <2 \\ y & <2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the truth set contains all tuples $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$ that satisfy this inequality. We can write the truth set $T$ of our predicate as follows:

$$
T = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \:|\: y < 2-x\big\}
$$

Finally, since $T$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^2,$ we can represent it as a region in the coordinate plane.

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ where $k$ is a constant such that $k\ne -1.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $det(A)\ne 0$

- **II.** $Ax=0$ has no solutions

- **III.** The lines $6x+2y=1$ and $-3x+ky=-2$ intersect at infinitely many points" :question/worked-solution "Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\cdot k-2\cdot (-3) \\  & =6k+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $6k+6\ne 0$ if $k\ne -1.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be a unique zero solution to $Ax=0.$

- Statement III is false. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

Finally, only statement I is true."} {:db/id 17592186262854 :question/id #uuid "364a18ef-2de8-57d7-9e2f-631eb4651446" :question/math-academy-id "q-127931"} {:db/id 17592186262856 :question/id #uuid \begin{aligned}\text{det}(H) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & \,\,\,-3 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 10 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 7 & \,\,\,-3 & 8 \\ 10 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 7 & \,\,\,-3 & 8 \\ 10 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the $1$st row of the $3\times 3$ determinant contains two zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(H) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 7 & -3 & 8 \\ 10 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(-6-0) \\  & =3\cdot (-6) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338735 :question/id #uuid "1cded5b0-233c-51be-b7fc-66e328db8e2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-69981"} {:db/id 17592186338736 :question/id #uuid "0e129d90-7991-5aeb-8e6d-b77b70757df7" :question/math-academy-id "q-69982"} {:db/id 17592186370953 :question/id #uuid "67a0d7e9-a72d-5fc5-b7f4-cd87aaa4ba3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-42923" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f91b8ff9-f8eb-51b8-b52f-289c02818338" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186370955} {:answer/id #uuid "f3e4a327-ea8e-530f-89f9-a4e243adc7d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186370956} {:answer/id #uuid "e926e6d7-8c6a-52a4-b903-1e9338a6f201" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186370957} {:answer/id #uuid "c331c706-c3f7-5678-9e57-a7714e5447c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186370958} {:answer/id #uuid "7ede5ce4-29de-59fd-baf2-447d94e15852" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186370959}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370955} :answer-field/id #uuid "59058239-7698-5829-8ac2-6fc0b1fe2dc4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186370954}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the determinant of the matrix

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=3$, which of the following statements are true? 
- **I.** $-4\text{det}({A}^{T})+2\text{det}(I)=3$
- **II.** $2\text{det}({A}^{T})=6$
- **III.** $\text{det}({A}^{T})-\text{det}(I)=1$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})=\text{det}(A)=3
$$

and

$$
det(I)=1.
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
-4\text{det}({A}^{T})+2\text{det}(I)=-4\cdot 3+2\cdot 1=-10\ne 3.
$$

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
2\text{det}({A}^{T})=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})-\text{det}(I)=3-1=2\ne 1.
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186329655 :question/id #uuid "4524ce2c-6b42-5e23-be24-247fd51db7f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-42482"} {:db/id 17592186329689 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=14$, and $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=-13$

- **II.** $-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-13$

- **III.** $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=-28$" :question/worked-solution "From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})=\text{det}(A)=14
$$

and

$$
det(I)=1.
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}3I & =3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a diagonal matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| & ={3}^{3}=27.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=14-27=-13
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-14+1=-13
$$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=14-14=0\ne -28
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and II only"."} {:db/id 17592186119932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119506 :question/id #uuid "a67e620f-6380-5754-81db-7e593cdf4336" 17592186274708}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

$$
a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,c=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10 \\ 0 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 7 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 5 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

Notice that the $1$st row of the determinant contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 7 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 5 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the $2$nd row of the $3\times 3$ determinant contains two zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =-2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot 4\cdot (-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =8|\begin{aligned}-2 & 10 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =8(-14+30) \\  & =128.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|128|=128.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186369845 :question/id #uuid "9fc304b0-a53d-5a62-b8cd-1ca341a43179" :question/math-academy-id "q-158367"} {:db/id 17592186369852 :question/id #uuid "47b0b8bf-3751-5718-9c72-c6b036aa4e92" :question/math-academy-id "q-158370"} {:db/id 17592186429818 :question/id #uuid "8d62e579-1b65-5746-996a-3e6e877f180c" :question/math-academy-id "q-158107" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119932 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3118d2af-771f-54c9-b18e-5196b87b6dca" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume of an N-Dimensional Parallelepiped"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3194d732-4a27-57e4-90b5-376278b1fad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "64" :db/id 17592186429806} {:answer/id #uuid "3c025708-e1f6-590a-bdc9-0995f51cbaec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "81" :db/id 17592186429807} {:answer/id #uuid "a745ff62-0494-5386-bded-3bb0f59f39cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "60" :db/id 17592186429810} {:answer/id #uuid "f1560774-e64f-5713-95be-58cfbace4e0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "70" :db/id 17592186429813} {:answer/id #uuid "fb522c79-1eec-53f4-a1ce-a41acd3ad978" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "53" :db/id 17592186429814}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f1560774-e64f-5713-95be-58cfbace4e0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "70" :db/id 17592186429813} :answer-field/id #uuid "0b729052-de1a-56fa-9f79-cc8f868046e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186429815}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

$$
a=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,c=[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 11 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 5 & 13 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. So, we have

$$
det(M)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 5 & 13 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=(-7)\cdot (-2)\cdot (-5)\cdot 1=-70.
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|-70|=70.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048462} {:db/id 17592186049530} {:db/id 17592186049875} {:db/id 17592186050376} {:db/id 17592186050308 :topic/difficulty 0.8258457054646602 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428372 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$" :question/worked-solution "From the parametric equation, we have that $v=⟨-2,8,0⟩$ and $w=⟨3,-1,-1⟩$ are parallel to the plane.

Now, we need to find a normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of $v$ and $w$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -2 & 8 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-8i-2j-22k \\  & =⟨-8,-2,-22⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨-8,-2,-22⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186311921 :question/id #uuid "8c5d0e74-0671-5cb7-b3b8-23383905b037" :question/math-academy-id "q-33819"} {:db/id 17592186311922 :question/id #uuid "6c4d4116-a9f1-5bf2-8a08-5f9441d405d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-33820"} {:db/id 17592186311923 :question/id #uuid "b724a31e-de81-5f97-aa9a-91e913632f49" :question/math-academy-id "q-33822"} {:db/id 17592186338862 :question/id #uuid "b2e1c378-a183-516b-92fd-1753dcbc375f" :question/math-academy-id "q-70972" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "027279ba-c86b-5b53-9b4f-d91a6c95b4d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,2,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186336052} {:answer/id #uuid "2b335037-3eda-5eb1-a665-40e27aacca2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-5,3,1⟩" :db/id 17592186336439} {:answer/id #uuid "3cc9ad4f-0956-53af-9375-a4dc1247e499" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-5,3,0⟩" :db/id 17592186336605} {:answer/id #uuid "924674c9-4ac4-5fac-bce9-febfcdbeeeee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨7,-3,1⟩" :db/id 17592186337359} {:answer/id #uuid "faf5ff12-8cff-5606-9806-8c51dfe352b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,-1,3⟩" :db/id 17592186338232}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336439} :answer-field/id #uuid "0006422d-58d9-51c7-8d8f-f4fd7450f036" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338278}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find a normal vector to the plane

:question/worked-solution "First, we need to find two vectors that are parallel to the plane (but not to each other). Let's use the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{DE}$ and $\overset{\to }{DF},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE} & =⟨-2,-2,5⟩-⟨1,0,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-2,7⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{DF} & =⟨-2,4,3⟩-⟨1,0,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we consider the position vector $d=⟨1,0,-2⟩$ of the point $D,$ then the corresponding parametric equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =d+s\overset{\to }{DE}+t\overset{\to }{DF} \\ r & =⟨1,0,-2⟩+s⟨-3,-2,7⟩+t⟨-3,4,5⟩,\,s,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=5 \\ 3s-t=-5 \\ 2s-t=-4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=5 \\ t=2 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =5 \\ -s+2(2) & =5 \\ -s+4 & =5 \\ s & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-1,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-b+2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-1)\cdot 2=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186241023 :question/id #uuid "caedc8c2-ba3c-5e61-ad1f-0d5eafbb8652" :question/math-academy-id "q-105257"} {:db/id 17592186241024 :question/id #uuid "1b477b81-717a-5a90-91d6-e069d7ac13b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-105261"} {:db/id 17592186241025 :question/id #uuid "8c4cb4f7-2d57-5ca9-8ffa-a4fe4548b0de" :question/math-academy-id "q-105265" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "145063fc-8e8e-5c5e-b9c0-4ce50643aeca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36" :db/id 17592186238221} {:answer/id #uuid "4fd14ba1-3c05-5721-9490-57e8bf80fea6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-42" :db/id 17592186238742} {:answer/id #uuid "a01540c4-5818-561d-9151-d28aeb0e7fe0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-39" :db/id 17592186239452} {:answer/id #uuid "b4e4047e-41ea-50d0-ab94-58e7363cb874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "60" :db/id 17592186239637} {:answer/id #uuid "ebdd9058-9132-5515-90b7-33b231320d45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-56" :db/id 17592186240131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238742} :answer-field/id #uuid "4dee8bc9-1a1f-59f0-8b66-162d23f34c3f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240468}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc,$ $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨-1,-1,4⟩$, $c=⟨-3,-8,14⟩$, and  $u=⟨5,-10,-14⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s-3t=5 \\ -s-8t=-10 \\ 4s+14t=-14\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ -1 & -8 & -10 \\ 4 & 14 & -14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -15 \\ 4 & 14 & -14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -15 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s-3t=5 \\ t=3 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
t=3.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s-3t & =5 \\ -s-3(3) & =5 \\ -s-9 & =5 \\ s & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-14,\,t=3,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-14b+3c.
$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 9 & k-6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-9{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & k-15\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-15.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k-15\,⇒\,k=15.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342229 :question/id #uuid "6c201285-f84a-584f-bd1b-b67204ad9977" :question/math-academy-id "q-74557"} {:db/id 17592186342230 :question/id #uuid "cef0a842-c20f-55db-9989-525f1aca72a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-74558"} {:db/id 17592186342231 :question/id #uuid "1691e3c5-722a-5803-9898-54e9fb9a633f" :question/math-academy-id "q-74559"} {:db/id 17592186342237 :question/id #uuid "e12a2efc-9d88-56c5-96b5-ec530d76269d" :question/math-academy-id "q-74594" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00ea0212-0c8f-50de-a9e9-986f267bdb5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186339138} {:answer/id #uuid "25b09d72-beeb-56f8-b3c5-bd45509568ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16" :db/id 17592186339451} {:answer/id #uuid "392acaa5-a047-5743-bd68-0e133d8bead9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186339642} {:answer/id #uuid "c4734975-ddc9-5119-b9e9-59e873e223ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-18" :db/id 17592186340873} {:answer/id #uuid "d55e6034-4f45-5b74-b206-75e90bc1aef4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186341016}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339138} :answer-field/id #uuid "690b25a1-892c-577b-b6f7-6ff437d6dcd1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341563}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where
