The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

![](images/d5/d51bdbe8820472334f7e1d942c027b6ad8164eaece58220f3f2e5cdb51544f05.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "bced0695-3ebd-5b62-b7ff-9c8f2500fc2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3921 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130067 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130396 :tutorial/content "A surface $z = f(x,y)$ is differentiable at a point $P$ if and only if it admits a *unique* tangent plane at $P.$ Intuitively, this means that, in the neighborhood of $P,$ the surface $z=f(x,y)$ can be approximated as a plane.

Note that this is analogous to the case of functions of one variable. A function $y = f(x)$ is differentiable at a point $P$ if and only if it admits a *unique* tangent *line* at $P.$ This is the same as saying that, in the neighborhood of $P,$ the curve $y=f(x)$ can be approximated as a straight line.  

We'll explore these ideas in more depth at the end of the lesson. For now, let's get some practice at computing tangent planes." :tutorial/id #uuid "015c4e8e-c1ba-5672-8228-ff0869681d6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4231 :tutorial/title "A Note on Differentiability"} :step/id #uuid "0296b5b5-c2ce-56c6-a8e4-ad0af71e0dde" :step/math-academy-id 25668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130046}} {:db/id 17592186130396 :tutorial/content "A surface $z = f(x,y)$ is differentiable at a point $P$ if and only if it admits a *unique* tangent plane at $P.$ Intuitively, this means that, in the neighborhood of $P,$ the surface $z=f(x,y)$ can be approximated as a plane.

Note that this is analogous to the case of functions of one variable. A function $y = f(x)$ is differentiable at a point $P$ if and only if it admits a *unique* tangent *line* at $P.$ This is the same as saying that, in the neighborhood of $P,$ the curve $y=f(x)$ can be approximated as a straight line.  

We'll explore these ideas in more depth at the end of the lesson. For now, let's get some practice at computing tangent planes." :tutorial/id #uuid "015c4e8e-c1ba-5672-8228-ff0869681d6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4231 :tutorial/title "A Note on Differentiability"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186407515} :activity/id #uuid "710af205-0718-5ccf-b346-4f23b266524d" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050293 :topic/id #uuid "3d717848-5743-5882-aa66-adea2ee38d55" :topic/math-academy-id 1980} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186407514 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342097 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52002c6b-9859-5b7b-a1de-586418b14736" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,3,28)$ only" :db/id 17592186339881} {:answer/id #uuid "551d2228-56ee-5488-91bb-0169794e5cbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-3,0)$ only" :db/id 17592186339910} {:answer/id #uuid "796a4945-abaa-5bd2-997d-087f2262b1b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,3,0)$ only" :db/id 17592186340210} {:answer/id #uuid "8a645bd4-5f4d-5164-aa70-44b211e15ecc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-3,0)$ and $(-1,3,28)$" :db/id 17592186340364} {:answer/id #uuid "c6b33a5b-7afb-5095-9268-a98f89267aca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-3,0)$ and $(3,1,20)$" :db/id 17592186340888}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339910} :answer-field/id #uuid "e58edcff-ee66-5f0c-86cd-1ec279fff31c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341787}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c589653c-432a-5bb8-acb2-94698429fbb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-73857" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y+6=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$
z={1}^{2}-2(1)+(-3)^{2}+6(-3)+10=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "0eadd7d5-26a1-573f-b533-83cfbfb498b9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407516}} {:db/id 17592186407515 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323964 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "464dff10-0c59-5dad-80a1-2ee16d60dbfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,-\pi ,2\pi )" :db/id 17592186321703} {:answer/id #uuid "48223b68-6d40-5d37-8bb5-b27364a9cf80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,\pi ,-1)" :db/id 17592186321715} {:answer/id #uuid "a226c677-0c51-577f-b0f5-1b3064cc6815" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\pi ,2,-2\pi )" :db/id 17592186322427} {:answer/id #uuid "adf98dbd-c12a-5550-9749-ddcc015f00fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,\pi ,12\pi )" :db/id 17592186322512} {:answer/id #uuid "d80a3e3a-b37d-53fa-b4ba-7e5d51839fdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,6,8\pi )" :db/id 17592186322836}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322427} :answer-field/id #uuid "5baf0726-2cff-5a6b-904f-2992e085ab37" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323351}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5c9333a9-b5d6-5ec8-b1f3-0c62768fb8b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-37986" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩=⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2c\operatorname{cos}⁡x-cy=8 \\ -xc=2\pi  \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-x(-2)=2\pi \,⟹\,x=\pi .
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $x=\pi $ into the first equation, we have 

$$
2(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-2)y=8\,⟹\,y=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\pi $ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -(\pi )(2) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(\pi ,2,-2\pi ).$"} :step/id #uuid "2b51d9b4-6f4d-519a-946f-18af30633fc4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407518}} {:db/id 17592186407516 :step/content {:db/id 17592186265748 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4831fde7-328b-5f95-8b4f-bd555404f79f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-1,4)" :db/id 17592186263624} {:answer/id #uuid "5b9d3b86-7aec-5970-92c9-47d3d544786f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,3)" :db/id 17592186263789} {:answer/id #uuid "94d3b3cb-73a3-5f94-abc9-28adc6612ba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,1,1)" :db/id 17592186264274} {:answer/id #uuid "9d20a40f-b237-5738-bfa6-76f889ea8789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3})" :db/id 17592186264345} {:answer/id #uuid "a54e3749-cf7d-5ffc-ac93-9256ee36c08f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{3},0,\frac{1}{9})" :db/id 17592186264415}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264345} :answer-field/id #uuid "38b8a09a-7de4-5c87-b2a5-460a354244c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "12830aeb-cb43-530e-902c-e52ba9d7524f" :question/math-academy-id "q-129557" :question/problem "At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=-\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)-2(y+1)-2(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2-2y-2-2z+2 \\ -2x+2y+2z+w+2 & =0 \\ 2x-2y-2z-w-2 & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,-2,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)^{2}-6(2)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1) & =4(2)(-2)+(1)^{2}=-15 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)(1)-3(2)^{2}=-16\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$

$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y-{z}^{2})=-2z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,0,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) & =-2(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) \\ w & =(x-1)+y-2(z-1) \\ w & =x+y-2z+1 \\ x+y-2z-w+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8189ee1b-e555-5395-af62-45720087b2f5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435557}} {:db/id 17592186435555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435553 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6521128c-8b33-54da-8c83-d27bef687244" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,1,-3)" :db/id 17592186435529} {:answer/id #uuid "6a9c4d22-52c4-582f-b256-0ddd6fa135ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},1,-\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186435530} {:answer/id #uuid "84cf53e7-7029-5a30-8dd0-ad54d0eb0064" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,2)" :db/id 17592186435533} {:answer/id #uuid "bcd79e5d-b439-5f83-a72f-40d75fd4cdd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,-1,-9)" :db/id 17592186435537} {:answer/id #uuid "d89ebc6c-8c25-5ee8-a102-c0421505fca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4})" :db/id 17592186435540}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435540} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1008d1e-ad25-59f1-8249-03f1bd3c30fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435547}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e0b70f07-48f3-5e91-bb4d-83ea4566f9c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-129560" :question/problem "At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=4y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨6,-8,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩=⟨6,-8,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2cx=6 \\ 4cy=-8 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2(1)x=6\,⟹\,x=3.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
4(1)y=-8\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=3$ and $y=-2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={3}^{2}+2(-2)^{2}-7 \\  & =9+8-7 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(3,-2,10).$"} :step/id #uuid "9be88cd8-1668-517f-a1dd-283be301d1d2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435555}} {:answer-field/choices :topic/math-academy-id 317} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065114 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065444 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we introduce a method of integration that can be used in cases where integration by substitution fails. The method is known as **integration by parts**. The so-called **by-parts formula** is 

$$
\int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x
$$

$$

In fact, that's precisely where it comes from!

To work out the formula, we recall the product rule for differentiation,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)=u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}+ v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x},
$$

where $u$ and $v$ are functions of $x.$ 

If we rearrange this formula a bit, we get

$$
u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)- v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Let's now integrate both sides of the equation:

$$
\int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x=\int\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)\,\textrm{d}x- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x
$$

Using the fundamental theorem of calculus, we can use the fact that $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)\,\textrm{d}x=uv,$ and we arrive at the by-parts formula:

$$
\int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x

$$

$$

Now, while the above is a mathematically correct statement, the integral on the right-hand side is *more* complicated than the integral we started with. Ouch!

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/a5/a50bf96047d64846b704a54ce965c9cf2c8c7916810b26849aacffe3ace84e60.png)

Consider the set $M,$ depicted by the shaded region above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is an interior point of the set $M$
- $B$ is a boundary point of the set $M$
- $C$ is an interior point of the set $M$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$ 

$$
{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

$$

$$

![](images/90/9072fe06b5821810a152f992cdd3d852ccb4cd0744c3a63119ba2634d3e3121d.png)

$$

$$

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $A$ is an interior point since there exists an open neighborhood of $A$ that is fully contained inside the set $M.$

- Statement II is true. The point $B$ is a boundary point because every open neighborhood of $B$ contains points that belong to $M$ and points that do not belong to $M.$

- Statement III is false. Every open neighborhood of $C$ contains points that belong to $M$ and points that do not belong to $M.$ The point $C$ is a boundary point for the given set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'."} {:db/id 17592186125215 :question/id #uuid "9e699ccb-274c-55bb-b36e-2ab5da35b953" :question/math-academy-id "q-71882"} {:db/id 17592186241034 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/c4/c4a50ae5f62dc5c52d0060a969d510453d3f922fad8f7ba887b2b1ee77fceae6.png)

Consider the set $M=(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )$ and the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is a boundary point of the set $M$
- $B$ is an interior point of the set $M$
- $C$ is an interior point of the set $M$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}\in R$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is *smaller than* $\delta :$ 

$$
{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

A neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is given by the open interval $({x}_{0}-\delta ,{x}_{0}+\delta ),$ shown below.

![](images/f8/f889352f25e7936d0e5ea76585a979efbb301da61f7e99a937e979af93ee0664.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The point $A$ is a boundary point because every open neighborhood of $A$ contains points that belong to $M$ and points that do not belong to $M.$

![](images/e8/e847aa005e917a88b19566933e3770edd05ddee946fc25dfd6fed91016bb909d.png)

- Statement II is false. The point $B$ is *not* an interior point of $M$ since any neighborhood of $B$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.

![](images/51/51439f6021efd768268e59c63627449cc68c9a420c4c7a80ab6773dd46e6ec1f.png)

- Statement III is true. The point $C$ is an interior point since there exists an open neighborhood of $C$ that is fully contained inside the set $M.$

![](images/dd/ddd471167f604b4ba97b36ddff3af6be7c7d3cfad6021a4cfc779c6f8ebb2a3d.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and III only.'"} {:db/id 17592186376110 :question/id #uuid "f55c2626-abbf-55a2-b039-2be6f6b0b944" :question/math-academy-id "q-159275"} {:db/id 17592186435511 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are given by

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y\le x+2},\,∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y=x+2}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The point $P(2,4)$ lies on the boundary of $A$
- **II.** The point $P(2,4)$ belongs to $A$
- **III.** The point $Q(-2,3)$ is an interior point of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie on or below the line $y=x+2.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](images/3b/3b0505f0c1fb295665dd64c9d0f26f23960b638ef0e1d414c7ad306a89154dfb.png)

Let's add the points $P(2,4)$ and $Q(-2,3)$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

![](images/62/623f00c423c7a846c52537d58c071c730083ba963fb488dbedbb76637ea9cc8c.png)

Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of $P(2,4)$ satisfy the equation $y=x+2.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $∂A,$ the boundary of $A.$

- Statement II is true. The coordinates of $P(2,4)$ satisfy the inequality $y\le x+4.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $A.$

- Statement III is false. Indeed, $Q$ is not an interior point of $A$ since any neighborhood of $Q$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only.'"} {:db/id 17592186376089 :question/id #uuid "7257b8a6-8ea5-5027-98d4-5845f1b59c79" :question/math-academy-id "q-158548"} {:db/id 17592186417816 :question/id #uuid "7e4c0564-b5b1-55bc-bc17-3dffa3a951a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-158601" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6fb12b54-0323-5408-9f63-bd359e7b2e14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453448} {:answer/id #uuid "164d2254-207a-594f-a70d-382d51b3f8e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453449}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453449} :answer-field/id #uuid "e5032cdf-c59e-5e33-880d-955f6d02841e" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454474} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3427dac4-97f1-5765-aafc-94068cf9677e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453450} {:answer/id #uuid "6c0ad7a7-e7bc-5678-aca2-5d4474e68307" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453451}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453450} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3387072-c1bc-59ee-8d45-dc6cd0e5411d" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454475} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "42ad1ee2-a34e-5097-bfd1-c65783c31fe4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453452} {:answer/id #uuid "0e0e000c-633e-51cc-bcaf-35de257a2bd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453453}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453452} :answer-field/id #uuid "feaa10ce-c2f4-5d9a-998c-4aa5896d0d74" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454476}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are given by

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y<-1},\,∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y=-1}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The point $P(1,-1)$ lies on the boundary of $A$
- **II.** The point $P(1,-1)$ belongs to $A$
- **III.** The point $Q(2,0)$ is an interior point of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie below the line $y=-1.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](images/75/75d5d199d12cc2f3170822a40c52762fcc8368caac26a8134661f9ac72ab462b.png)

Let's add the points $P(1,-1)$ and $Q(2,0)$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

![](images/81/818da293be040897d3a536b396d6fe7ff992f3d91f976301e14a6253356b5bde.png)

Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of $P(1,-1)$ satisfy $y=-1.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $∂A,$ the boundary of $A.$

- Statement II is false. The coordinates of $P(-1,1)$ do not satisfy the inequality $y<-1.$ Hence, $P$ does not lie in the set $A.$

- Statement III is false. Indeed, $Q$ is not an interior point of $A$ since any neighborhood of $Q$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.

{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie above the line $y=2x-3.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the coordinates of $Q(0,0)$ satisfy the inequality $y>2x-3.$ Hence, $Q$ lies in the set $A.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, there exists an open neighborhood of $Q$ that is entirely contained inside the set $A.$

:topic/math-academy-id 1930} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125863 :tutorial/content "A **neighborhood** of a point $x_0\in \mathbb R$ is the set of points that are "close to" $x_0.$ 

More precisely, let's define a number $\delta >0$, where $\delta$ is usually very small.  A **neighborhood** of a point $x_0$ is the set of all points whose distance from $x_0$ is smaller than $\delta.$ 

In one-dimensional space, a neighborhood of a point $x_0\in\mathbb R$ is an open interval $\left(x_0-\delta, x_0+\delta\right),$ shown below.

![](images/04/04016c37be4c907eabc144db16eb757dff773907262ccd04941cf27ddd2e49d6.png)

For example, if we set $\delta = 0.1,$ then the corresponding neighborhood of the point $x_0 = 2$ is as follows:

![](images/03/0329bef56b8b903eb13510b7344fd7ca488d34c8d0c85c7648cebc8ecf7cfa40.png)

Note that $x=1.9$ and $x=2.1$ are *not* included in this neighborhood since their distance from the point $x_0$ is *not* smaller than $\delta.$ 

We can represent a neighborhood of $x_0$ using set notation as follows:

$$
\{x : | x- x_0| < \delta \}
$$

We often refer to sets of this type as *open* neighborhoods since they contain all points whose distance from $x_0$ is *smaller than* (but not equal) to $\delta.$" :tutorial/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 41433 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125607}} {:db/id 17592186125607 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125864 :tutorial/content "In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of a point $\mathbf x_0\in \mathbb R^2$ is a disc of radius $\delta$ centered at $\mathbf x_0$ that does not include the bounding circle, as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

The definitions of the interior and boundary points are the same as for the one-dimensional case. The only difference is that now a neighborhood of a point is a disc.

For example, consider the set $S$ and points $A,$ $B, C,$ and $D,$ shown below.

![](images/a7/a7e037fd998c235ff7b721e7187d44814700ac5f41a256920f34f248c798c520.png)

Let's classify each of these as interior or boundary points (or neither):

- $A$ is an interior point since *there exists* a neighborhood of $A$ that is fully contained inside the set.

- $B$ is neither an interior nor a boundary point because *there exists* a neighborhood of $B$ that does not contain points from the set.

- $C$ is a boundary point since *every* neighborhood of $C$ contains points that lie in the set and points that do not lie in the set.

- $D$ is a boundary point since *every* neighborhood of $D$ contains points that lie in the set and points that do not lie in the set.

Notice that although $C$ and $D$ are both boundary points, $C\notin S$ and yet $D\in S.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bfda97a2-2fe7-5c9a-a067-dbf903ba2111" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6825 :tutorial/title {:db/id 17592186125622 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125870 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that $S$ is a set of real numbers. A point $x_0$ is called an **interior point** of $S$ if *some* neighborhood of $\mathbf x_0$ is *fully contained* inside $S.$ 

For example, consider the set $S=[0,1)$ and the points $A$ and $B,$ shown below.

![](images/a1/a12c60b6f60ca7c35162fb1ddf0d0d507fe80e73e621c451c21f0b882034ae21.png)

The point $A$ is an interior point of $S,$ but $B$ is not:

- The point $A$ is an interior point of $S$ since there exists a neighborhood of $A$ that is *fully contained* inside $S.$

- The point $B$ is *not* an interior point of $S$ since there is no neighborhood of $B$ that is *fully contained* inside $S.$ In other words, any neighborhood of $B$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.

Note that neither $x=0$ nor $x=1$ are interior points. To see why, let's draw a neighborhood of each point:

![](images/a9/a923732241443a0fd6a5f53dab7de2d346f5704a0b034c276e64dc3df2746f4f.png)

 

From here, we can deduce the following:

- The point $x=0$ is *not* an interior point of $S$ since there is no neighborhood of $x=0$ that is *fully* contained inside $S.$

- The point $x=1$ is also *not* an interior point of $S$ since there is no neighborhood of $x=1$ that is *fully* contained inside $S.$

The set containing all interior points of a set $S$ is called the **interior** of $S,$ and is denoted $\textrm{int}\,S.$ 

For the set $[0,1),$ its interior is given by

$$

More precisely, let's define a number $\delta >0$, where $\delta$ is usually very small.  A **neighborhood** of a point $x_0$ is the set of all points whose distance from $x_0$ is smaller than $\delta.$ 

In one-dimensional space, a neighborhood of a point $x_0\in\mathbb R$ is an open interval $\left(x_0-\delta, x_0+\delta\right),$ shown below.

![](images/04/04016c37be4c907eabc144db16eb757dff773907262ccd04941cf27ddd2e49d6.png)

For example, if we set $\delta = 0.1,$ then the corresponding neighborhood of the point $x_0 = 2$ is as follows:

![](images/03/0329bef56b8b903eb13510b7344fd7ca488d34c8d0c85c7648cebc8ecf7cfa40.png)

Note that $x=1.9$ and $x=2.1$ are *not* included in this neighborhood since their distance from the point $x_0$ is *not* smaller than $\delta.$ 

We can represent a neighborhood of $x_0$ using set notation as follows:

$$
\{x : | x- x_0| < \delta \}
$$

We often refer to sets of this type as *open* neighborhoods since they contain all points whose distance from $x_0$ is *smaller than* (but not equal) to $\delta.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b2ea7b59-5287-5d12-b53f-32a9254b8ba7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6818 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "44c26f5a-57b1-5e3b-b126-e2f92e8f7bac" :step/math-academy-id 41386 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125622}} {:db/id 17592186125863 :tutorial/content "A **neighborhood** of a point $x_0\in \mathbb R$ is the set of points that are "close to" $x_0.$

Consider the set $M,$ depicted by the shaded region above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is a boundary point of the set $M$
- $B$ is an interior point of the set $M$
- $C$ is a boundary point of the set $M$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

$$

$$

![](images/be/be1ece00243777f3f6b6973319e15ea1e5c8556b2452b61a451713f9dcb86595.png)

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $A$ is a boundary point because every open neighborhood of $A$ contains points that belong to $M$ and points that do not belong to $M.$

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7e4c0564-b5b1-55bc-bc17-3dffa3a951a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-158601" :question/problem "The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are given by

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y<-1},\,∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y=-1}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The point $P(1,-1)$ lies on the boundary of $A$
- **II.** The point $P(1,-1)$ belongs to $A$
- **III.** The point $Q(2,0)$ is an interior point of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta }
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie below the line $y=-1.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](images/75/75d5d199d12cc2f3170822a40c52762fcc8368caac26a8134661f9ac72ab462b.png)

Let's add the points $P(1,-1)$ and $Q(2,0)$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

![](images/81/818da293be040897d3a536b396d6fe7ff992f3d91f976301e14a6253356b5bde.png)

Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of $P(1,-1)$ satisfy $y=-1.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $∂A,$ the boundary of $A.$

- Statement II is false. The coordinates of $P(-1,1)$ do not satisfy the inequality $y<-1.$ Hence, $P$ does not lie in the set $A.$

- Statement III is false. Indeed, $Q$ is not an interior point of $A$ since any neighborhood of $Q$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only.'"} :step/id #uuid "b1e2a497-e042-518c-bac4-15b77f002a69" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417820}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+7y=-\operatorname{sin}⁡pt,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Which value of the parameter $p$ causes the oscillator to resonate?" :question/worked-solution "The equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $1.$ Therefore,
$\omega =1.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =1$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(2D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(2C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]+t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2D\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2C\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only solution I matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186231576 :question/id #uuid "a2dc0571-7d63-58c4-a7e9-b264e1dac3a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-343760" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cac41120-247d-5821-b7f6-b342dbcf8f18" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8588f05c-f259-5f6f-95a4-ba743efb8633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186230323} {:answer/id #uuid "87e2a5ac-5e6b-5176-ada3-76165f3827b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186230324} {:answer/id #uuid "bd0f684b-31be-53dd-959a-4c693200fbd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186230325} {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad71e63-ab40-5319-b40d-20fec2c9d4de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186230327}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6c1fc5b-ecb6-509b-ab8e-ba64d464ed59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186230322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. $$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-1$ and $D=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Only solution III matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."} {:db/id 17592186435718 :question/id #uuid "9d091e55-28a6-57e1-bec5-20aeba4179e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-343770"} {:db/id 17592186435720 :question/id #uuid "f5e9f5eb-87cf-56db-acd3-a7af3f0549dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-343755" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8098c12c-c69f-5410-91ea-5d34faacac72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474792} {:answer/id #uuid "cbf8c1e6-7440-5b66-ac6a-a95e969d0c0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474793} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0703231-e8db-5753-a623-8cdd5ed3035a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475322} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ebb008e-2a78-528f-b65f-04738d8d69bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474794} {:answer/id #uuid "3b5fb8cd-1e60-5d1a-9b3c-43f1bdfb0eee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474795}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474794} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ee39774-5b22-57d7-b22d-32c67ba80ab1" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475323} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "154527e1-d8e6-580a-bfa6-88b0d7e11c16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474796} {:answer/id #uuid "fe8f9ab4-11d0-5d2b-b95a-f6633b354687" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474797}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474797} :answer-field/id #uuid "80d02f47-2169-5889-be5d-7762353c0de6" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475324}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

The external force is $f(t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $2.$ Therefore,
$\omega =2.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$

$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =2$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[4(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)]+4t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 4D\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4C\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{7}{4}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

Only solutions I and III match the forms above.

$$
y''+\omega^2y=f(t),
$$

where $\omega$ is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation $y''+\omega^2y=0$ and $y_p$ is any particular solution to the full equation.

Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}$

Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form

$$
f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),
$$

so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

A sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ would duplicate $y_c,$ so at resonance we multiply by $t$ and use a trial of the form

$$
y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

To determine $C$ and $D,$ we first compute derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+t(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t))-t{\omega }^{2}(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the equation, we have that the $t$-terms cancel out, and we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}{y}_{p}=2\omega D\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)-2\omega C\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we need $y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),$ equating coefficients gives

$$
2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},
$$

so a standard resonant particular solution is

$$
y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

So, when $f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)$ and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b19a33b7-fd81-538c-8139-d44653c47533" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14777 :tutorial/title "General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "35c65152-fe66-57ca-8c82-a01849b005d7" :step/math-academy-id 612654 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231834}} {:db/id 17592186231834 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231295 :question/id #uuid "f41473ff-05a6-5f3e-ae5b-0584810aa0dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-21878"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cac41120-247d-5821-b7f6-b342dbcf8f18" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231571} {:db/id 17592186231576} {:db/id 17592186317427} {:db/id 17592186317429} {:db/id 17592186317430} {:db/id 17592186317431} {:db/id 17592186317432} {:db/id 17592186317433} {:db/id 17592186427272} {:db/id 17592186435718} {:db/id 17592186435720} {:db/id 17592186442740}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations"} :step/id #uuid "eb6f14ff-8487-50a4-a45b-1ff02e60483d" :step/math-academy-id 612655 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231835}} {:db/id 17592186231835 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231988 :tutorial/content "Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of $t$). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases *without bound*.

For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator

$$
y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).
$$

The complementary solution is of the form $y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),$ the natural frequency of the system is $\omega = 3,$ and the forcing frequency is also $3.$ Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

Since the forcing term $\sin(3t)$ duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by $t.$ We try a solution of the form $y_p = t(C\cos(3t) + D\sin(3t)).$

Calculating the derivatives of $y_p,$ substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of $\sin(3t)$ and $\cos(3t)$ yields $C=-\dfrac16$ and $D=0.$ So, the particular solution is of the form

$$
y_p = -\dfrac{t}{6}\cos(3t).
$$

Notice that this solution grows larger as $t$ increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.

In real systems, perfectly *unbounded growth* does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude. where $\omega$ is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation $y''+\omega^2y=0$ and $y_p$ is any particular solution to the full equation.

Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}$

Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form

$$
f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),
$$

so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

A sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ would duplicate $y_c,$ so at resonance we multiply by $t$ and use a trial of the form

$$
y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

To determine $C$ and $D,$ we first compute derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+t(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t))-t{\omega }^{2}(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the equation, we have that the $t$-terms cancel out, and we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}{y}_{p}=2\omega D\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)-2\omega C\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we need $y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),$ equating coefficients gives

$$
2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},
$$

so a standard resonant particular solution is

$$
y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

So, when $f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)$ and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b19a33b7-fd81-538c-8139-d44653c47533" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14777 :tutorial/title "General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "35c65152-fe66-57ca-8c82-a01849b005d7" :step/math-academy-id 612654 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231834}} {:db/id 17592186231987 :tutorial/content "Consider an undamped forced oscillator,

In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of $t$). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases *without bound*.

For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator

$$
y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).
$$

The complementary solution is of the form $y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),$ the natural frequency of the system is $\omega = 3,$ and the forcing frequency is also $3.$ Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

Since the forcing term $\sin(3t)$ duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by $t.$ We try a solution of the form $y_p = t(C\cos(3t) + D\sin(3t)).$

Calculating the derivatives of $y_p,$ substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of $\sin(3t)$ and $\cos(3t)$ yields $C=-\dfrac16$ and $D=0.$ So, the particular solution is of the form

$$
y_p = -\dfrac{t}{6}\cos(3t).
$$

Notice that this solution grows larger as $t$ increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.

In real systems, perfectly *unbounded growth* does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude. Even so, forcing near the natural frequency can still produce very large oscillations, which is why resonance is important in engineering design." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f439c3c-eac7-5d41-a8b1-fcbe2eb8d44b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14778 :tutorial/title "Practical Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "d14184e9-93ef-5eca-99aa-b25660380309" :step/math-academy-id 612658} {:db/id 17592186231988 :tutorial/content "Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2595439f-c010-51c2-987d-b6e986cd13da" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441794}} {:db/id 17592186441793 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317422 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cca9f77e-1eac-5dd3-b2b8-a6a15bf83357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{18}{5}" :db/id 17592186316277} {:answer/id #uuid "282a52cc-8658-5a56-b555-abd92b1826a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.6" :db/id 17592186441790}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186316277} :answer-field/id #uuid "6fa88ca7-4486-52c4-a8ca-dfdd856acf42" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186316816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7756f2f0-f8ff-5a38-a573-589b8cc562e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343691" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-1$ and $D=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$

$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{8}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)=2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $3.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "83ab17b5-350b-529d-97cb-ee01d416ef71" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442745}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f62d1759-0498-58c4-ab55-caa874c6319e" :answer/type {:db/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ee642054-1d27-50a4-8f05-345ca578dfc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-343743" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[9(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 9D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{2}{3}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} :step/id #uuid "c4c6cf6d-8b3b-5c57-b551-475a3ee53347" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442741}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10ac45f2-8682-5e38-90a5-af6b3b0df052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186442734} {:answer/id #uuid "720de89b-25be-516b-9df5-32bca90894e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186442735} {:answer/id #uuid "8b3b3ddc-f2b0-5960-a120-6e3182615388" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186442736} {:answer/id #uuid "90774d44-8df7-5a01-b829-eff4553b5ba9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186442737} {:answer/id #uuid "eb5401b3-3249-566f-8e5f-01020ae0590b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186442738}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442736} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3260424-876c-50ae-ac8b-7b96731c9907" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442739} {:answer/id #uuid "10ac45f2-8682-5e38-90a5-af6b3b0df052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186442734} {:answer/id #uuid "720de89b-25be-516b-9df5-32bca90894e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186442735} {:answer/id #uuid "8b3b3ddc-f2b0-5960-a120-6e3182615388" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186442736} {:answer/id #uuid "90774d44-8df7-5a01-b829-eff4553b5ba9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186442737} {:answer/id #uuid "eb5401b3-3249-566f-8e5f-01020ae0590b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186442738} {:db/id 17592186048337 :topic/difficulty 1.0 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429319 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. - The set $A$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. For instance, $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $x-4y=1$ since $0-4\cdot 0=0\ne 1.$

- The set $B$ is a subspace. It represents a plane, and a plane is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $x=-2y$ since $0=-2\cdot 0.$ So $0$ lies in $B.$

- The set $C$ is not a subspace. No point in ${R}^{3}$ satisfies the equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}<0.$ Hence, $C=∅.$ The empty set is not a subspace since it does not contain the zero vector.

"q-35575" :question/problem "Which of the following sets is a subspace of ${R}^{2}?$

I. $A=\{⟨x,y⟩\in {R}^{2}:y=0\}$

II. $B=\{⟨x,y⟩\in {R}^{2}:y=3x\}$

III. $C=\{⟨x,y⟩\in {R}^{2}:y=2\}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is a subspace. It represents a line, and a line is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $y=0$ since $0=0.$ So, $0$ lies in $A.$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following sets are neither open nor closed?
- **I.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2\le x\le 6,\,0<{y}^{2}\le 3}$
- **II.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<{x}^{2}<9,\,1<{y}^{2}<16}$
- **III.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0\le y\le {x}^{2},\,-2\le x\le 2}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(2,\sqrt{3}).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(2,0).$

- The second set is *open* since it doesn't contain any point of its boundary (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

- The third set is *closed* since it contains all its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186241058 :question/id #uuid "9d461bff-0ae1-55fc-a03d-01dfa63c39ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-105437"} {:db/id 17592186338993 :question/id Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- **II.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1}$
- **III.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }-1<x<1,\,1<y<3-{x}^{2}}$

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *open* since it doesn't contain any of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

- The second set is *closed* since it contains all of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

- The third set is *open* since it doesn't contain any of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

For example, consider the set depicted below. It's a disc, and its boundary is a circle.

![](images/87/874837c21e81d1e0aa68220fb49275ea9e2a0b4f1fc990c18fb36816eb28779c.png)

Remember that a closed set contains all its boundary points, while an open set contains none of its boundary points.

- The set above is not closed because it does not contain all of its boundary. On the left side of the graph, the circular boundary is dashed, meaning it is not contained within the set.

- The set above is not open because it contains some of its boundary. On the right side of the graph, the circular boundary is solid, meaning that it is contained within the set.
